*Klassenarbeit*German{}from German;Klasse,Arbeit,|Pronunciation}/ˈkla.sənˌar.baɪ̯t/+/ˈkla.sən.arˌbaɪ̯t/}Ⓓ8/84/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#school written class test,exam|Usage notes}are the most formal kind of exams in German schools. They are usually announced some time in advance and their number per semester and subject is fixed (at school level and,with regard to minima and maxima,at state level). They also have a fixed influence on a pupil's mark,typically 25 percent per exam. Additional,less formal exams are called Test,Abfrage,or the like.}From year 11 onwards,are usually called Klausur instead,which is also the term used at universities.

*Knacklaut*German{}|Etymology}knacken+Laut|Pronunciation}/ˈknakˌlaʊ̯t/}Ⓓc/cf/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^s][s][es])}#phonetics glottal stop}•synononym:[Glottisschlag],[Glottalplosiv],[Kehlkopfverschluss],[Kehlkopfverschlusslaut]}#especially a glottal stop found in null onsets (vowel-initial stems) in German and other languages|Usage notes}It is often claimed that Standard German automatically inserts a glottal stop in null onsets,but this is a myth. Any initial glottal stop may be elided in everyday speech. While such pronunciations may be considered substandard,they by themselves belie the claim of an ''automatic'' glottal stop. More importantly,however,glottal stops in ''unstressed'' onsets are entirely optional and more often than not elided even in formal,careful standard speech.

*knebeln*German{}|Etymology}17th century,derived from Knebel,from Middle High German @-1,from Old High German knebil. The word originally meant a stick used to tighten a tie or to bind something to,later also the tie itself. from Dutch knevelen shows the same semantic development,being used chiefly for “to gag”,but also in the broader sense “to tie up”.|Pronunciation}/ˈkneːbəln/}Ⓓf/f3/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#transitive to gag Literally:[tie a piece of cloth around someone’s mouth to prevent them from shouting]}#transitive to hog-tie Literally:[tie up someone’s arms and legs to prevent them from moving]}#}@^ An Händen und Füßen '''ge@-1t''',der Mund verklebt,verscharrt in einem Papp-Sarg – ein Horror!}•'''Hog-tied''' at your hands and feet,adhesive tape over your mouth,buried in a cardboard coffin—a horror!}#transitive to hog-tie; to render helpless; to oppress; to enslave|Usage notes}Most dictionaries give only the sense “to gag”,but the sense “to hog-tie” is attestable from Early Modern German to the present. Often both ideas also go hand in hand,especially in the combination gefesselt und ge@-1t. Note that fesseln as such is broader in meaning,as it can also mean “to handcuff” or “to tie to something immovable”,which  never does.|Derived terms}Knebelvertrag

*Knifte*German{}|Etymology}From Knift,a word found in several Central German dialects,sometimes meaning "large knife",sometimes "slice of bread". The word meaning "knife" is probably derived from Middle Low German knîf,also from Middle High German knîf (West Central German),both from Proto-Germanic ⋆knībaz (whence also from English knife). The sense "rifle" can be explained from this via "weapon" or "bayonet". The word meaning "slice of bread" may be identical (via "cut off"),or otherwise a related form.|Pronunciation}/ˈknɪftə/}Ⓓa/a2/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(fem.)}#military rifle}#colloquial thick slice of bread

*Knofi*German{}|Etymology}A diminutive form pertaining to Knoblauch. The ''-f-'' is due to its being derived from dialectal forms. One would expect a from German Low German - origin (cf. from Middle Low German knoflōk),but there are also forms with ''-f-'' in some southern German dialects (themselves from Old High German chlovalouh). Southern origin is more likely given the regional form Knofel,but Low German would have helped to spread the form in the north.|Pronunciation}/ˈknoːfi/}/ˈknoːvi/,(less common)|Noun}(mask.)}#colloquial garlic}•synononym:[Knoblauch<g:m)],[;],[Knofel (southern Germany],[ Austria)<g:m)]

*Knoten*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German knote,from Middle High German knode,from Old High German knoto,from Old High German knodo.}The two forms are probably variants based on Grammatischer Wechsel. The form with ''-t-'' (from Proto-Germanic ''}-d-'') was predominant in East Central German,that with ''-d-'' (from Proto-Germanic ''}-þ-'') in Upper German. Incidentally,this situation explains the lengthened vowel in the standardized form (lengthening being blocked before ''-t-'' in Upper German,but not in Central German). Neither German form can be derived directly from Proto-Germanic ⋆knuttô,whence from Middle High German knotze and from English knot,though a relation is very likely.}The senses “journeyman”,“person (of some quality)” are probably due,at least in part,to conflation with from Middle Low German mate,companion,cognate of Cognate German Genosse. Alongside,there is a common tendency of referring to people,especially children,with words for thick,plump,or inflated objects (compare e.g. Balg).|Pronunciation}/ˈknoːtən/+ˈknoːtən+ˈknoːtn̩}Ⓓ9/98/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.,diminituve:[@^Knötchen])}#knot Literally:[looping]}#knot Literally:[swelling]}#Austria interchange Literally:[motorway junction]}#nautical knot Literally:[unit of speed]}#graph theory vertex,node}#obsolete craftsman; journeyman; farmhand}#in compounds a person of some specified quality or practice; chiefly in l+de+Furzknoten,but sometimes other colloquial formations|Synonyms}sense:interchange Dreieck; Autobahndreieck; Kreuz; Autobahnkreuz}sense:in graph theory Ecke|Hyponyms}Autobahnknoten}Fruchtknoten}Gordischer @^}Haarknoten}Nervenknoten}Schuhbandknoten|Derived terms}knotig

However,there is a strong tendency to use the verb only for the preparation of a proper dinner,be it lunch or supper. Hence,the preparation of,say,an onion tart for dinner is ,even though the food is baked. Contrarily,the preparation of breakfast is only rarely called  even if eggs are boiled in the process.}Transitive  can generally be used only for actual boiling. *kommste heut nicht, kommste morgen*German{}|Alternative forms}less common; rendered in formal Standard German|Etymology}Literally:[if you don't come today,you'll come tomorrow].}Some sources trace it back to Colognian m:küss de hück nit,küss de morje,but the saying is attested in various dialect dictionaries. (Colognians are by stereotype easygoing and workshy,which may be the reason for the association.) Compare also cog:kom ik er vandaag niet,dan kom ik er morgen.|Pronunciation}/ˌkɔmstə ˈhɔʏ̯t nɪç(t) ˌkɔmstə ˈmɔʁɡən/|Phrase}#expresses a hands-off,easygoing attitude,especially with respect to time; depending on the context it may be positive/neutral or negative (then implying tardiness or unreliability)}•Du hast noch 60 Euro auf deinem Deckel! Aber kein Stress:'''Kommste heut nicht,kommste morgen.'''}•You still have 60 euro on your slate! But no worries:You can pay it whenever you have it on you.}•Die Busse fahren hier nach der Devise:'''Kommste heut nicht,kommste morgen.'''}•

*Kran*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German krane,from Old High German tcrane,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆kranō,from Proto-Germanic tcrane.}The word was used metaphorically for the lifting device due to the similar appearance of the bird’s neck and head. This metaphorical use is first attested in from Middle Dutch krane,and thence spread to several European languages (compare from English crane,from French grue). The sense “water tap” is restricted to a smaller territory (compare from Dutch kraan,from Luxembourgish Krunn).|Pronunciation}/ˈkʁaːn/}Ⓓc/c6/De-@^.ogg}Rhymes:aːn|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[^e][e])}#crane Literally:[a lifting device]}•Bei Sturm darf ein '''@^''' nicht umfallen.}•A '''crane''' must not fall over in the event of a storm.}#regional tap,faucet}•synononym:[Hahn],[Wasserhahn],[Pipe]}•Der '''@^''' in der Küche tropft.}•The '''tap''' in the kitchen is dripping.|Derived terms}@^eberger|Descendants}}:}:

*Kretscham*German{}2018|Etymology}From Middle High German kretscheme,from a from German - language,from Proto-Slavic ⋆kъrčьma. Doublet of Kaschemme.|Pronunciation}/ˈkrɛt͡ʃam/}Ⓓ7/78/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(mask.)}#Silesia a village inn or tavern}#}• Ich schloy mich och biß weeln im ganzen '''Kratschem'''  mit Knaichten unde Bouren rümm unde mache doß der Balbir unde der Bader ze thun/unde de Gerichte ze besichtigen bekummen.}#}• Am Trauungstage war Sammlung  d. h. die Gäste des Bräutigams versammelten sich Nachmittags im Gerichts'''kretscham'''  nahmen einen Trunk Bier  ließen solchen auch den anderen Anwesenden  Nichthochzeitsgästen  reichen. Auch dem dabei nicht anwesenden Pfarrer wurden einige Kannen Bier gut geschrieben. Aus dem '''@^''' ging man nun ins Brauthaus  wo der Hochzeitbitter als Redner auftrat; von da zog man feierlich  oft unter Glockengeläute  oft mit vorangehender Musik in die Kirche. Braut und Bräutigam wurden jedes von 2 sogenannten Brautführern an das Altar geleitet und nach der Trauung zurückgeführt; auch hatten beide Brautleute Züchtjungfern  kleine  auch mit Kränzen geschmückte Mädchen. Wie in die Kirche  zog aus derselben man zurück ins Hochzeitshaus  meist das Haus der Braut. Dort waren die Tische schon gedeckt  man setzte sich bald  nicht in bunter Reihe  sondern nach Geschlechtern und genoß eine Menge von Gerichten. War der Pfarrer anwesend  so sprach er das Tischgebet  sonst der Hochzeitbitter und stundenlangen Sitzen wurde das Essen mit dem Gesange eines Liederverses  gewöhnlich:Lob und Ehr und Preis ꝛc. und vorher gesprochenem Gebete  beschlossen. Dann hielt der Hochzeitbitter im Namen der Brautleute eine Dankrede  an deren Schlusse er zum Beschenken des Brautpaares aufforderte  auch zum sogenannten Bierzuge  d. h. er lud ein in den '''@^''' zu ziehen  was Herrschaft und '''@^'''besitzer fordern konnten  doch mit dem Zusatze:„Wem es sein Amt  oder Stand  oder sonst etwas nicht gestattet  wolle sichs noch länger bei Speise und Trank im Hochzeithause gefallen lassen. Im '''@^''' waren noch viele Personen anwesend  freien Trunk erwartend  und nicht blos die Brautleute  sondern auch die Hochzeitsgäste ließen fleißig einschenken. Hatte man bei der Hochzeit Musik  so wurde im '''@^''' auch getanzt.|Derived terms}@-2mar,@-2mer

*Krug*German{}|Pronunciation}/kruːk/}/kruːx/,(northern and central Germany) now chiefly colloquial}Rhymes:uːkuːx|Etymology 1}From Middle High German kruoc,from Old High German kruog,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆krōgu,from Proto-Germanic ⋆krōguz. Immediate cognates are from Middle Dutch croech,from Old English crōg,of obscure origin. Possibly from a from Proto-Indo-European - root shared with from Old Armenian pitcher,large jar,from Ancient Greek pitcher,but the phonetics are problematic.  Also compare from Old Irish skin.}The originally Low German Kruke,cognate with from English crock,is another word,though a relation with ''@^'' is considered likely.|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[Krüge],diminituve:@^)}#jug}•synononym:Kanne|Etymology 2}From Middle Low German krôch,from Middle Low German krûch,whence from German Low German Kroog and through borrowing from Dutch pub,from Swedish krog. Further origin unknown. A relation with etymology 1 cannot be ruled out,but is considered unlikely by most authorities.|Noun}(mask.,genitive:@^es,plural:[Krüge])}#dated pub; bar}•synononym:Kneipe (see there for further synonyms)|Usage notes}The simplex has now become rare. The compound Dorfkrug remains in use for the central pub or inn of a village. The word is also still found in the names of many traditional pubs in northern Germany.|Derived terms}Nobiskrug

*Kuchen*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈkuːxən/+ˈkuːxn̩+ˈkuːχn̩+-ən}Ⓓ/4/45/De-@^.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}Ⓓ/1/13/De-@^2.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}LL-Q188 (deu)-Sebastian Wallroth-@^.wav(Germany)}Ⓓ/9/9c/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)|Etymology 1}From Middle High German kuoche,from Old High German kuohho,from Proto-Germanic ⋆kōkô. Compare from Dutch koek. from German Quiche.|Noun}(mask.,diminituve:@^)}#pie; cake; tart Literally:[foodstuff made of baked dough,other than bread]|Usage notes}can refer to almost any foodstuff that is made of dough,baked in a pan or oven,and considered fit for consumption by itself (unlike bread). Which sorts are in fact called  and which are not,is mainly a matter of tradition,for which no clear rule can be given. For example,Pizza is not included in the term,unlike the rather similar Zwiebelkuchen and Flammkuchen. While most  have pieces cut from them,the northern German Schmalzkuchen are bite-sized. *Kugel*German{}'''@^n'''|Pronunciation}/ˈkuːɡəl/|Etymology 1}}From Middle High German kugel,from Middle High German kugele,of from German nocap1 origin,but probably related to Keule.}de Possibly from Proto-Germanic tknobbed instrument,a derivative offrom Proto-Germanic tcog,swelling,from Proto-Indo-European tswelling,bow,an extension of from Proto-Indo-European tto bow,bend,arch,curve”,whence also perhaps from Albanian tacorn,small ball.}Further discussion}Outside of loans from German (as in from Danish kugle and from Dutch kogel),it appears only in German,and only from the Middle High German period,as ''kugel,kugele'',referring to a ball used in games (Spielkugel).}Nevertheless,the word seems to be of genuinely from German - origin. A Swiss dialect form has an additional ''r'',in ''krugle'',found already in Middle High German in the diminutive form ''krúgellin'' (Konrad of Würzburg,d. 1287).}Middle German variants of the word in the original sense “ball used in skittles or Paille-maille” are ''kaule,kulle'',while Low German had cognates of Klotz.}The sense “bullet” is directly via comparison with the ball in skittles,already in use for lead or iron spheres used as projectiles (fired with slingshots or similar) before firearms became widespread.}Also compared are Kegel,as well as from English cudgel and from English cog,though these connections are far from certain.}{{rel-bottom|Noun}(fem.,diminituve:@^)}#ball defdate:13th century}#firearms bullet,projectile defdate:15th century}•synononym:[Projektil],[Geschoss]}•Die '''@^''' ging mitten ins Herz.}•The '''bullet''' went right through the heart.}#firearms round,cartridge,bullet}•synononym:Patrone}•Er hatte noch drei '''@^n''' im Magazin.}•He had three '''rounds''' left in the magazine.}#astronomy orb,globe,celestial body defdate:16th century}#geometry sphere,orb defdate:16th century}•synononym:Sphäre}#heraldiccharge roundel of any tincture}#of icecream scoop|Usage notes}The German words ''@^'' and Ball are distinguished inasmuch as the former refers to solid balls (such as those used for billiards or bowling) while the latter refers to air-filled or elastic balls (such as tennis or soccer balls). This distinction may be neglected colloquially or jokingly.|Derived terms}kugeln}kugelig}kuglicht}verkugeln|Hyponyms}Babykugel}Bowlingkugel}Erdkugel}Glaskugel}Gewehrkugel}Halbkugel}Kristallkugel}Mottenkugel}Schrotkugel}Christbaumkugel}Weihnachtskugel}Weihnachtsbaumkugel}Weltkugel}Zielkugel|Noun}(fem.)}#alternative form of [Kogel]

*Kupfernickel*German{}|Etymology}From @-6,(copper)Nickel,(mischievious spirit or demon). This word originated as a pejorative German term for ores of the element nickel,whose bright green color closely resembles malachite,an otherwise reliable indicator of valuable copper ore. However,like iron,nickel ore is impossible to smelt at the relatively low temperatures needed to smelt copper. (This is also why the Copper Age preceded the Iron Age.) Annoyed at wasting their time on such ore,German miners began calling it <i>cupfernickel</i>,that is,"copper demon." When chemists eventually identified and named the element in the ore,they shortened the name of the ore to <i>nickel</i>. The name of this element thus has the same roots as the phrase "Old Nick," which refers to a supreme devil or demon. Feeling a bit whimsical,chemists of that same period named another newly isolated iron-like element,cobalt,after a mischievous German household spirit,the "kobold."|Noun}(neut.)}#cupronickel

*KZ*German{}|Etymology}The expected initialism KL was used officially at least in the earlier years of the National Socialist concentration camps. While it is not entirely clear how the informal variant &_ originated,it is usually thought that it came to be preferred and eventually standardised due to its sounding harsher. A possible origin is from the fact that the common German pronunciation of Konzentrationslager contains the cluster ts,predominantly represented in German by the letter Z,three times:ˌkɔn.'''ts'''ɛn.tʁaˈ'''ts'''joːn'''ts'''ˌlaːɡɐ. *Lagemaß*German{}|Etymology}Lage|Pronunciation}^Ⓓe/e1/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(neut.)}#statistics central tendency}#}• Das '''''@^''''' besteht aus einer einzigen Zahl  die den repräsentativsten Wert Ihrer Daten widerspiegelt. ('''Central tendency''' describes a single number that aims to give you a sense of the most representative value in your data. *Lallname*German{}|Etymology}From lallen,(babble) prattle,Name,(name). A technical term in onomatology,first coined in 1896 (for ancient Greek) by Paul Kretschmer,''Einleitung in die Geschichte der Griechischen Sprache'',p. 334. Used for German names by A. Socin,''Mittelhochdeutsches Namenbuch'' (1903).|Noun}(mask.,plural:[@^ns.weak])}#onomastics a hypocoristic form of a given name which is phonologically simplified in child language but enters adult use. Especially in ancient names of Asia Minor (in Anatolian languages such as Phrygian,Luwian,Hittite),but also used for other languages.

("in the context of ''Waltharius'',c. AD 920 the long-sword spatha was worn on a baldric on the left hip,the half-sword scramasax on the right,usually attached to the mail-shirt hauberk with chains.") *Lappen*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈlapən/}ˈläpən,ˈläpm̩,(standard)}ˈla̝(ʔ)m̩,(Northern Germany)}ˈlɑp.pən,(Swiss)|Etymology 1}From Middle High German lappe,from Old High German lappo,from Proto-West Germanic tcloth,rag,lobe of from German nocap1 origin,possibly from Proto-Indo-European to hang loosely.}The form is remarkable because of the unshifted geminate ''-pp-'' (instead of expected Old High German}''lapfo''). Based on the supposedly invariable nature of the consonant shift,from Old High German lappo would have to be an originally Central and Low German form (compare from Old Saxon lappo). This is,however,quite unlikely since the Old High German word is attested as early as the 9th century,and no variants with ''-pf-'' exist. *lassen*German{}|Alternative forms}obsolete|Etymology}From Middle High German lāzen,from Old High German lāzan,from Proto-West Germanic tto let,allow,from Proto-Germanic to leave behind,allow,from Proto-Indo-European to let,leave behind. Cognates include from Bavarian låssn,from Dutch laten,from English let.|Pronunciation}ˈlasn̩+ˈlasən}Ⓓ/2/2b/De-@^.ogg(Germany)(Germany)}Ⓓ/5/5d/De-at-@^.ogg(Austria)(Austria)}las+sen|Verb}@^(lässt#ließ,ge@^:@^with an infinitive)}#transitive to allow; to permit; to let}•lasset alle Hoffnung fahren}•abandon all hope}#auxiliary to have someone (do something); to have (something done); to make (something happen); to cause (something to be done)}•Wir haben neue Schränke für die Küche machen '''@^'''.}•We '''had''' new cabinets made for the kitchen.}•Hast du dir die Haare schneiden '''@^'''?}•Did you '''get''' your hair cut?}•Ich '''ließ''' den Nachbarn die Blumen gießen. (active) - Ich '''ließ''' die Blumen (vom Nachbarn) gießen. (passive)}•I '''made''' the neighbor water the flowers. - I '''had''' the flowers watered (by the neighbor).}#transitive to let remain,to leave (in a certain state)}•Mir ist es lieber,meine Haare grau zu '''@^'''.}•I prefer to '''leave''' my hair grey.}#transitive to stop (something); to quit; to refrain from; to help doing (something)}#intransitive to cease; to desist|Usage notes}Note that the English phrases "to ''let'' someone do something" and "to ''make'' someone do something" both translate into German as ''jemanden etwas tun @^''. In order to avoid ambiguity,"to let" can be expressed as ''jemandem erlauben,etwas zu tun'' or ''zu@^,dass jemand etwas tut'',while "to make" can be expressed as ''jemanden dazu bringen,etwas zu tun'' or ''dafür sorgen,dass jemand etwas tut''.}In perfect tenses,''@^''+infinitive takes a double-infinitive construction,i.e. both verbs are in the infinitive:''Ich habe mir die Haare schneiden @^.'' (“I’ve had my hair cut.”). This was the original sense in Middle High German,and this is still common in Bavaria and Austria. But descriptions or definitions that claim it has only this meaning are contradicted by long-established usage. In fact,''@^'' is neutral with regard to pace in modern German,unless the context implies it,as in:}Regardless of pace,moreover,only  is commonly used of animals and in such idioms as  or m:tto learn to walk.}In Austria,however,''@^'' is not considered neutral with regard to pace,and a strict distinction is made between gehen,which is exclusively used in the sense of “to walk”,and ''@^'' and rennen,both of which are exclusively used in the sense of “to run”.|Derived terms}ab@^}Amok @^}an@^}auf dem Laufenden}auf Hochtouren @^}auf@^}aus dem Ruder @^}aus@^}be@^}davon@^}durch@^}ein@^}eis@^ or Eis @^}entlang@^}ent@^}er@^}Gefahr @^}herab@^}herauf@^}heraus@^}herein@^}her@^}herüber@^}herum@^}herunter@^}hinab@^}hinauf@^}hinaus@^}hinein@^}hin@^}hinüber@^}hinunter@^}ins Leere @^}ins Messer @^}ins offene Messer @^}Lauf}Läufer}läufig}leer@^}los@^}mit@^}nach@^}rauf@^}raus@^}rein@^}rüber@^}rum@^}über@^}um@^}unter@^}ver@^}voll@^}vor@^}weg@^}wund@^}zer@^}zu@^}zurück@^|See also}gehen}rennen

*lebendig*German{}|Etymology}From Middle High German lëbendic,from Old High German lëbēntīg. Equivalent to @-2+ig.}The word originally had normal stress on the initial syllable,as is still the case in from Dutch levendig,from Yiddish לעבעדיק,and in some dialectal German forms such as from Hunsrik levendich. The shift to the second syllable is first attested in the 16th century; it had established itself as the sole standard by the mid-18th century.<ref name"Weigand">Weigand,''Deutsches Wörterbuch'' (1860)</ref> While such shifts happened more often in modern German (compare Forelle,Holunder,Wacholder),the case of  is peculiar in that it is a transparent formation rather than a word whose derivation had become obscure.|Pronunciation}/leˈbɛndɪç/+le-+lə- qualifier:standard}Ⓓ7/7a/De-@^2.ogg}/leˈbɛndɪk/qualifier:common form in southern Germany,Austria,and Switzerland}Ⓓ2/2d/De-@^.ogg}Ⓓ1/12/De-@^3.ogg|Adjective}#living,alive,animate}•synononym:[@-2],[am Leben]}#lively,vivacious,spirited,animated,vibrant,active,agile}•synononym:lebhaft|Derived terms}quick@^}spring@^

*lehnen*German{}|Pronunciation}/ˈleːnən/}Ⓓ7/71/De-@^.ogg}Lehnen |Etymology 1}From a merger of two interrelated verbs:.}#from Middle High German linen,from Middle High German lenen,from Old High German hlinēn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hlinēn,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hlināną}#from Middle High German leinen,from Old High German hleinen,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆hlainijan,from Proto-Germanic ⋆hlainijaną,a causative of the former.}The merger occurred in Central and Low German dialects,in which ''-ei-'' and open-syllable ''-i-,-e-'' all become > ''-ē-'' (from Middle Low German lēnen). *-lein*German{}|Alternative forms}-el}-li}-lin}-elein|Etymology}From Middle High German -elīn,from Middle High German -līn,from Old High German -ilī,from Old High German -ilīn,from Proto-West Germanic ⋆-ilīn. Cognate to from Dutch -lijn.|Pronunciation}/laɪ̯n/}^Ⓓd/d5/LL-Q188_%28deu%29-Frank_C._Müller-@^.wav|Suffix}#suffix used to create a diminutive form; e.g. ''Kind'' → ''Kind'''lein'''''|Usage notes}In contemporary Standard German,is usual with words whose stems end in ''-ch'' or ''-g''; thus more often Bächlein than Bächelchen. There is a limited number of other forms that remain in common use,but for the most part  now has a poetic and archaic tone. The general diminutive suffix in the written language and in northern speech is -chen,while southern informal use prefers regional suffixes like -le,-li (Swabian/Alemannic) and -erl (Austro-Bavarian).}Diminutives in  generally have umlaut. The endings  are all deleted before the suffix.}The plural remains unchanged. However,a few nouns with a plural in -er may carry the same ending over to the plural diminutive,and a few diminutives referring to people allow a plural in .
